sections.html:
Fairfield County is home to Danbury, roughly 50 miles northeast of New York City. Residents numbered 86,518 in 2020, seventh among Connecticut cities. The city measures 44.19 square miles, with 41.95 of that land. The town government merged into the city in 1965, so assessment and collection for the whole area run through one set of city offices.

Danbury is organized into named districts instead of one grid, among them Mill Plain, Great Plain, Long Ridge, Germantown, Beaverbrook and Wooster Heights. A house on Long Ridge Road and another near downtown are worlds apart in a buyer's eyes, and an appraiser will price them accordingly. Known as the Hat City for its old hat industry, Danbury now draws buyers who commute on Interstate 84 or on the Metro-North Danbury Branch, which ends here.

sections.h2: How Danbury property tax is billed
sections.html:
The real estate bill arrives in July. The city's real estate FAQ lets a bill over $100 be paid in four pieces, due in July, October, January and April, while smaller ones are paid whole. The July piece covers July, August and September.

The assessment date is October 1 of the previous year. The FAQ illustrates it with a buyer who closed in January 2010 and still owed the bill built on the October 2009 list: assessed in arrears, paid current. Call the Tax Collector for the installment rules that apply now. A deed filed with the Town Clerk prompts the Assessor to change the owner's name and address on the parcel.

sections.h2: Who does what at City Hall
sections.html:
• Assessor: values, appeals and changes of address.
  • Tax Collector: bills, payments and the payoff figure.
  • City Council: the mill rate, voted every May.

Sending each question to the right desk saves several calls. Payoff goes to the collector, value to the assessor, and the rate is settled by the council vote in May.

sections.h2: How does the five-year revaluation work?
sections.html: Values are redone every five years. The latest revaluation fixed them for the October 1, 2022 Grand List, and bills at the new values first came due in July 2023. A revaluation is revenue neutral, so the city's total levy does not change, but individual bills shift, some up and some down. The Assessor's 2022 revaluation page warns owners not to estimate taxes using the prior year's mill rate.

To contest a value, petition the Board of Assessment Appeals. The board's page makes clear that the applicant's evidence is all it weighs. Saying the value is too high, with nothing behind it, counts for nothing, and comparable sales must be adjusted.

sections.h2: What winter does to a Danbury house
sections.html:
Winters are cold and snowy here and summers hot and humid. A season brings 49.3 inches of snow on average, and about 56 inches of precipitation falls over the year, 3 to 5 inches in every month. Inspectors hired by buyers tend to start with three things.

  • Roof: snow weighs on it and ice can back up under shingles, so its age comes up on nearly every inspection.
  • Heat: a tired furnace or boiler is a cost buyers can see coming after a long winter.
  • Water: expect questions about drainage, sump pumps and damp basements.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax when you sell?
sections.html:
At closing, any Danbury tax still owed is normally taken from the seller's proceeds. Talk to the Tax Collector and the closing agent about how the payoff will work for your account. Several missed installments do not block a sale, since the title company subtracts the balance and sends you the remainder.

The July bill can land on either side, depending on the contract and the settlement statement. It rides on the October 1 assessment and a July due date, and the title company usually prorates it. Request that the Danbury number be itemized. If the closing falls between installments, the split is worth checking twice, because it is the line where sellers and buyers most often disagree.

The state wants a conveyance tax return when the deed is recorded. Under Department of Revenue Services guidance, the grantor, or the grantor's attorney or agent, files Form OP-236 when the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies. Danbury's three-digit town code on the form is 034.

  • Sales can be filed electronically through myCTREC if the town takes part.
  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence is an exempt conveyance.
  • A principal residence is also exempt when the price cannot cover the mortgages plus the tax and sewer liens that rank ahead of them.

The closing agent can tell you if an exemption fits.

sections.h2: What Danbury sellers usually run into
sections.html:
Three themes recur among Danbury sellers: aging systems, tenants in multi-unit houses and tax bills paid in installments.

  • A house built before the 1970s may need roof, heating or electrical work before a financed buyer's lender will proceed.
  • An inherited house can have several unpaid installments, and because the list date is October 1, the first bill after a sale may carry the previous owner's name.
  • Landlords near downtown or the university may be selling with a lease already running.

Any of the three can make an as-is cash sale the shorter road. The buyer accepts the house as it is, and tax comes out of the proceeds through the title company.

sections.h2: A short plan for Danbury sellers
sections.html:
If your Danbury house is going on the market, start with the October 1 list, because that is the date every bill follows. Find out which installments are paid, call the Tax Collector for a payoff figure, and ask the Assessor whether any appeal window is open. Next, gather the deed, any lease and notes on the roof, the heating system and basement moisture. Then decide between listing and a cash sale based on how much repair work the house needs and how long you can wait for a buyer's loan to clear.

If you choose cash, the sequence is simple. The buyer looks at the house and makes an offer. The title company checks ownership, tax and any liens, and the conveyance tax return is prepared for the deed. At closing you sign, the balance owed is paid, and you receive the rest. Keep a copy of the settlement statement and the recorded deed.

faqs.q: How many installments is Danbury property tax paid in?
faqs.a: Four for a bill above $100: July, October, January and April. Bills of $100 or less are paid whole. Confirm today's rules with the Tax Collector.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Danbury assessment?
faqs.a: Applications are due in February each year. In-person filings must be date stamped by 6:00 pm on the deadline, and mailed ones stamped by the Postal Service, not a meter. Ask the Assessor for the exact date.

faqs.q: When was the last Danbury revaluation?
faqs.a: The last one set values for the October 1, 2022 Grand List, with new bills due from July 2023. Connecticut requires a revaluation every five years.

faqs.q: What town code is used for Danbury on the state conveyance form?
faqs.a: On Form OP-236 the Danbury town code is 034.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Danbury house with tax still owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays unpaid tax out of the proceeds at closing, so you do not need to bring money to the table.
